# Scientific Writing {#sec-scientific-writing}

A research paper is the instrument through which a discovery becomes knowledge.
A result that is not written down does not exist scientifically; a result written
badly exists only for the handful of readers willing to excavate it. This chapter
treats scientific writing not as cosmetic polish applied after the "real" work but
as an integral part of the research itself—a design problem with its own
constraints, its own failure modes, and its own measurable quality. The audience
is the marketing scholar who has a finding and now faces the harder task of
convincing a skeptical editor, two or three adversarial reviewers, and an
indifferent field that the finding is correct, novel, and important.

The economics of the situation are unforgiving. The top journals in marketing—the
*Journal of Marketing* (JM), the *Journal of Marketing Research* (JMR),
*Marketing Science*, and the *Journal of Consumer Research* (JCR), collectively
the "top-4"—desk-reject a large share of submissions and ultimately accept only a
small fraction of what is sent to them. <!-- CITE-NEEDED: top-4 marketing journal acceptance/desk-reject rates -->
A reviewer reads dozens of papers a year as unpaid labor and forms a judgment
within the first few pages. The paper that survives is not merely the one with the
best result; it is the one whose argument the reviewer can reconstruct without
effort and whose contribution the reviewer can state in a sentence. Writing is
therefore a competitive technology, and this chapter develops it as one.

The chapter proceeds from architecture to sentence. We begin with the **structure**
of a paper—the canonical section sequence and what each section is for—and formalize
the underlying logical scaffold. We then treat the hardest and most consequential
task, **framing the contribution**, and then the two genres the hypo-deductive
template serves badly—the **descriptive paper**, which contributes a pattern, and
the **abductive paper**, which reasons from a pattern to the best available
explanation. Next comes the part of the paper where framing
lives or dies: the **front end** (title, abstract, introduction). We turn next to
the specific demands of writing for the **top-4**, where the contribution bar is
highest. We close with **clarity and revision**: the sentence-level craft that
makes an argument legible, the measurement of readability, and the disciplined
process of responding to reviewers. Throughout, the stance is the house stance—
intuition first, then the formal structure that makes the intuition operational.

## The Structure of a Paper {#sec-sw-structure}

### The canonical sections and their tenses

Empirical marketing papers share a near-universal skeleton, sometimes abbreviated
**IMRaD** (Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion) with literature review
and conclusions bracketing the core. Each section answers one question and only
one, and—this is a point novices routinely miss—each section has a *default verb
tense* that signals the epistemic status of its claims. Completed actions take the
**simple past** ("we estimated", "respondents rated"); established knowledge and
the paper's own ongoing argument take the **present** ("the effect is", "Table 2
reports"); prior literature as a stream that continues into the present takes the
**present perfect** ("researchers have shown"). @tbl-sw-sections collects the
sections, their purposes, approximate lengths, and tense conventions.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sw-sections
#| tbl-cap: "Canonical sections of an empirical marketing paper, with purpose, indicative length, and default verb tense. Lengths are rules of thumb for a full-length top-4 submission, not hard limits."
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(knitr)
sw_sections <- data.frame(
  Section = c("Title", "Abstract", "Introduction", "Literature / Theory",
              "Methods", "Results", "Discussion", "Conclusion"),
  `Words` = c("8–15", "200–250", "800–1200", "1500–3000",
              "1000–2500", "1000–2500", "1500–2500", "400–800"),
  Purpose = c("Name the contribution",
              "Self-contained summary: objective, method, finding, implication",
              "Why the paper exists; the gap and the contribution",
              "Position vs. prior work; derive hypotheses or model",
              "What was done, reproducibly",
              "What was found, with the data doing the talking",
              "What it means, limits, boundary conditions",
              "Restate contribution; implications and future work"),
  `Default tense` = c("—", "Past + present", "Present + present perfect",
                      "Present + present perfect", "Past", "Past + present",
                      "Present + past", "Present"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(sw_sections)
```

The discipline of one-question-per-section is what gives a paper its navigability.
A reader who wants to know *what you did* turns to Methods and finds only that; a
reader who wants to know *why it matters* turns to the Discussion and is not
detained by procedure. Violations—results smuggled into the methods, mechanism
speculation buried in the results—are the most common structural defect flagged in
review, because they force the reader to hold the paper's logic in their head
rather than read it off the page.

> A scientific paper is not a chronological record of what the researcher did. It
> is a reconstructed argument, organized so that the reader can verify the
> conclusion with minimum effort. The order of discovery and the order of
> exposition are different things, and conflating them is the surest route to an
> unreadable manuscript.

### The argument as a logical object

Underneath the section skeleton sits a logical scaffold that the prose merely
dresses. Make it explicit. A confirmatory empirical paper advances a chain

$$
\underbrace{P}_{\text{problem}} \;\Rightarrow\;
\underbrace{G}_{\text{gap}} \;\Rightarrow\;
\underbrace{H}_{\text{hypotheses}} \;\Rightarrow\;
\underbrace{D}_{\text{design}} \;\Rightarrow\;
\underbrace{R}_{\text{results}} \;\Rightarrow\;
\underbrace{C}_{\text{contribution}}
$$ {#eq-sw-chain}

in which every arrow is a claim the reader can refuse to grant. The problem $P$
must be real (someone cares about the answer); the gap $G$ must be genuine (the
answer is not already known); the hypotheses $H$ must follow from a theory and be
falsifiable; the design $D$ must be capable of discriminating $H$ from its
negation; the results $R$ must actually bear on $H$; and the contribution $C$ must
be what $R$ licenses, not more. A paper fails at whichever arrow is weakest, and
the writing task is to make each arrow as short and as forced as possible. Many
rejections that are phrased as "not enough contribution" are in fact broken
arrows: a gap that turns out to be already filled ($G$), or a design that cannot
separate the focal hypothesis from a confound ($D \not\Rightarrow R$).

The conceptual or theory paper substitutes a different chain—a construct is
defined, related to existing constructs, and shown to do explanatory work—but the
demand for unbroken arrows is identical. @fig-sw-paper-flow renders the canonical
flow and shows where each link in @eq-sw-chain is forged.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-sw-paper-flow
%%| fig-cap: "The logical flow of an empirical paper. The front end (title, abstract, introduction) carries the problem, gap, and promised contribution; the body discharges the promise. A reviewer reads the front end to decide whether the rest is worth reading."
flowchart TD
    A["Title<br/><i>names the contribution</i>"] --> B["Abstract<br/><i>P → R → C in 250 words</i>"]
    B --> C["Introduction<br/><i>problem P, gap G,<br/>promised contribution C</i>"]
    C --> D["Theory / Literature<br/><i>position; derive H</i>"]
    D --> E["Methods<br/><i>design D</i>"]
    E --> F["Results<br/><i>evidence R</i>"]
    F --> G["Discussion<br/><i>does R license C?</i>"]
    G --> H["Conclusion<br/><i>restate C; boundaries</i>"]
    C -.->|"promise"| G
    H -.->|"payoff"| C
    style C fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#1a73e8
    style G fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#1a73e8
```

The dashed promise–payoff loop in @fig-sw-paper-flow is the structural heart of a
paper. The introduction makes a promise—"we will show that $X$ causes $Y$ through
mechanism $M$"—and the discussion must redeem exactly that promise, no more and no
less. A paper that promises a causal claim and delivers a correlation, or that
delivers a richer finding than it promised and never updates the framing, reads as
incoherent even when every individual sentence is sound.

### Paper types

The skeleton flexes with the paper's type, and naming the type early orients both
writer and reviewer. Four types recur. A **research paper** tests hypotheses and
reports findings; its contribution lives in $H \Rightarrow R$. A **methods paper**
proposes a new estimator, design, or measurement instrument; its contribution is
that the method recovers something prior methods could not, so the burden is a
demonstration—often on synthetic data with known ground truth—that it works and a
comparison against incumbents. A **review paper** consolidates a domain, and its
contribution is organization: a taxonomy, an integrative framework, or an agenda
that practitioners and scholars did not previously have. A **conceptual or
discussion paper** advances or critiques theory, trading empirical evidence for
argumentative rigor. The reviewer evaluates each type against a different
standard, and a paper that does not signal its type invites evaluation against the
wrong one.

## Framing the Contribution {#sec-sw-contribution}

### What a contribution is

The single most important sentence in a paper is the one that states its
contribution, and the most common reason good work is rejected is that this
sentence is missing, vague, or overclaimed. Define the contribution formally.
Let $\mathcal{K}$ denote the field's existing knowledge—the set of claims a
competent reader already accepts before reading the paper. A paper's contribution
is the increment

$$
\Delta\mathcal{K} \;=\; \mathcal{K}_{\text{after}} \setminus \mathcal{K}_{\text{before}},
$$ {#eq-sw-contribution}

the set of claims that a reader is licensed to accept *after* reading the paper and
was not licensed to accept before. Three properties make $\Delta\mathcal{K}$
publishable, and reviewers probe each one explicitly:

- **Novelty** ($\Delta\mathcal{K} \neq \varnothing$): the increment is non-empty.
  If every claim in the paper already belonged to $\mathcal{K}_{\text{before}}$,
  there is no contribution, however well executed the study.
- **Validity** ($\Delta\mathcal{K}$ is warranted): the increment is actually
  licensed by the evidence and argument. Overclaiming—asserting elements of
  $\Delta\mathcal{K}$ that the design $D$ cannot support—is the fastest route to a
  reviewer's "the conclusions outrun the data".
- **Importance** ($|\Delta\mathcal{K}|$ matters): the increment is one the field
  cares about. A true, novel, but trivial claim clears the first two bars and fails
  the third, and "importance" is precisely the bar that rises from a field journal
  to the top-4.

Two broad species of contribution recur in marketing, and a paper should know which
it is making. A **substantive** contribution changes what we believe about a
marketing phenomenon—that brand prominence signals status through quiet versus loud
cues, say, or that responding to online reviews trades complaint quantity for depth
(see @sec-branding). A **methodological** contribution changes how we can learn
about phenomena—a new identification strategy, a scalable text measure, a more
efficient estimator. The strongest papers often pair a methodological advance with
the substantive finding it unlocks, but a paper that is fuzzy about which kind of
increment it offers will be read as offering neither.

### The contribution statement and the framing trap

A contribution should be expressible as a single declarative sentence of the form
"We show that [claim], which prior work did not establish because [reason], using
[design]." The clause "which prior work did not establish" is the gap $G$ of
@eq-sw-chain made explicit, and it must be *true*: nothing destroys credibility
faster than a literature-savvy reviewer who knows the claimed gap was filled years
ago. Conversely, a contribution can be undersold. Authors who have lived inside a
problem for years often state their finding in the narrow terms in which they
discovered it, missing the more general claim the evidence actually supports. The
discipline is to state the *most general* claim that $R$ licenses and not one inch
more.

Framing is the act of choosing which $\mathcal{K}_{\text{before}}$ to write against—
which conversation the paper joins—and it is a genuine strategic choice, not a
neutral description. The same result can be framed as a contribution to several
literatures, and the framing determines the reference set, the reviewers, and the
perceived importance. A study of how customers respond to a salesperson's language,
for instance, could be framed against the persuasion literature, the
frontline-service literature, or the computational-text-analysis literature, and
the right choice depends on where the increment $\Delta\mathcal{K}$ is largest and
the audience most receptive. The **framing trap** is to choose the literature in
which the result is *most surprising* rather than the one in which it is *most
defensible*; surprise attracts an editor's eye but invites reviewers who hold the
strongest priors against the claim.

### Setting Up a Question Whose Answer Is Not Already Known {#sec-sw-open-question}

The framing trap above has a constructive counterpart. A paper is read when its
question is genuinely open—when a well-informed reader, having finished the
introduction, could not confidently guess the result. Most manuscripts fail this test
in the first two pages, and the usual reason is that they motivate with a *gap* rather
than a *question*. "Prior work has not examined $X$" tells the reader that something
is missing, invites the reply that it may be missing for good reason, and quietly
promises that $X$ will turn out to matter. Everyone knows how that paper ends.

The strongest available move is to assemble two established literatures that imply
*opposite* answers, or that block the two obvious remedies, and then let the data
adjudicate. @tanlamai2026housing is a compact instance, and it is worth reading as a
piece of construction rather than for its result (@sec-aiml-genai-housing).

The setup takes two moves. First, decades of evidence establish that houses in
white-dominant neighborhoods sell above otherwise-similar houses in minority-dominant
neighborhoods, and the literature attributes the gap to *human* bias. The implied
remedy—take the human out of the loop—is the reader's own next thought, which is
exactly why the second move lands: recent work shows the gap is not fixed by
conventional AI models, including those designed specifically to address
discrimination. *Machine* bias closes the escape route that human bias opened.

With both remedies blocked, "what does a generative model do here?" becomes a
question a reader cannot answer from the armchair. A case runs each way. Generative
models are trained on human-produced text and should inherit human bias; they are also
statistical predictors and should inherit the proxy encoding that defeats conventional
models. Yet they represent a property differently than a hedonic regression over
neighborhood features does, and it is not obvious that the same proxies survive that
representation. The paper reports that generative AI *narrows* the gap—and the finding
is interesting only because the framing made both directions live beforehand.

Three rules generalize from this.

**Both branches must be publishable before you know which one you have.** Write the
question so that each answer is a contribution, ideally as an explicit pair: *if the
gap narrows, then $X$; if it widens, then $Y$*. If only one branch is a paper, the
introduction is doing advocacy, and reviewers detect this even when they cannot name
it. This is also the honest form of the framing: it is what you would have
pre-registered.

**A counter-intuitive result raises the evidentiary bar rather than lowering it.**
Surprise is not a contribution by itself; it is a debt. The reader's first hypothesis
is that something is wrong with the measurement, so a paper of this shape owes a
mechanism section, and owes it as a real analysis rather than a paragraph of
speculation (@sec-causal-mediation, @sec-sw-emb). Papers that lead with a surprising
headline and defer the mechanism to "future research" are the ones that fail to
replicate.

**The two literatures must be summarized in terms their own authors would accept.**
The move degrades into a straw man the moment either position is flattened to make the
opposition sharper. The workable test: write your one-sentence characterization of
each literature, and ask whether a proponent would sign it. If either would object,
the tension you have constructed is between caricatures, and a referee drawn from that
literature will be the one to say so.

## The Descriptive Paper {#sec-sw-descriptive}

The template assumed so far—theory, hypotheses, identification, test—is not the
only publishable shape, and treating it as such quietly rules out a class of
papers the field needs. A **descriptive paper** establishes what a phenomenon
*looks like* without claiming to have identified a causal effect within it. Its
increment $\Delta\mathcal{K}$ consists of pattern claims: this outcome
co-occurs with that antecedent, this population sorts into these categories,
this quantity has moved this way over this period.

The genre has explicit methodological warrant. @helfat2007stylized argues that
stylized facts are a legitimate and necessary input to theory development,
because a theory can only be built against a phenomenon whose shape is known.
@hambrick2007devotion goes further, arguing that the field's insistence on a
theoretical contribution in every paper suppresses precisely the descriptive
work theory needs to feed on. Neither position licenses atheoretical
data-dumping: @suttonstaw1995 is equally clear that data, variables, and
diagrams are not themselves theory. The reconciliation is that a descriptive
paper contributes a *pattern*, states it as a pattern, and lets the theoretical
payoff be the discipline the pattern imposes on subsequent explanation.

@choudhury2026abduction supply the positive account. Abduction—the mode of
inference that formulates candidate explanations for an unexplained
phenomenon—is a distinct research design rather than a deduction that failed to
find support. Their treatment distinguishes the *abductive trigger* (the
anomalous observation that starts the inquiry) from *creative* abduction
(generating candidate explanations) and *selective* abduction (winnowing them),
and is explicit that abduction admits no fixed template. That absence of a
template is exactly why descriptive papers need to make their design visible on
the page: a reader cannot infer it from convention.

### What makes a descriptive contribution defensible

Five design choices separate a descriptive paper that publishes from one that
reads as a set of cross-tabulations. @tbl-sw-descriptive states them alongside a
worked example: @moeen2026valuecapture, which maps founder knowledge origin onto
mode of economic value capture in U.S. medical device start-ups and is developed
substantively in @sec-entrepreneurship.

| Design choice | Why it matters | In the worked example |
|:--|:--|:--|
| The outcome is a **category**, not a magnitude | A mode question ("which market does the venture monetize in?") has no natural causal counterpart, so description is the right design rather than a consolation prize | Value captured in the market for technology, the market for product, or not at all |
| The antecedent variation is **institutionally sharp** | A boundary drawn by an institution rather than by the researcher forecloses the "you defined the groups to get the result" objection | Founders who were academic scientists vs. former employees of within-industry firms |
| The **typology is declared before the data** | A pattern claim can only be wrong—and therefore only be informative—if the correspondence it predicts was specified in advance | Scientific vs. commercial knowledge dimensions, crossed with founder origin |
| The outcome categories are **externally classified** | Descriptive work dies when the dependent variable rests on the author's judgment calls | IP transactions and FDA clearance leave a regulatory paper trail |
| The **off-diagonal case is reported** | The cell that violates the clean mapping is what distinguishes a mechanism from a stereotype; in a design with no treatment, it does the work an interaction term would do elsewhere | Founders bridging both dimensions shift to pioneering products rather than following their institution |

: Five design choices that make a descriptive contribution defensible, with a worked example. {#tbl-sw-descriptive}

The fifth row deserves emphasis because it is the one most often omitted. A
descriptive paper that reports only the clean correspondence has documented a
stereotype: academics do this, employees do that. The reader has no way to tell
whether the operative variable is the credential or the knowledge. Reporting the
cases that break the correspondence, and showing that they break it *in the
direction the proposed mechanism predicts*, converts the pattern into an
explanation candidate. This is selective abduction performed in public.

### How the contribution sentence changes

The contribution sentence of @sec-sw-contribution still applies, with the causal
verb removed and the boundary stated. Rather than "we show that $X$ causes $Y$,"
a descriptive paper claims "we establish that $X$ and $Y$ correspond in
population $P$, which prior work had not documented because it lacked
[data/classification/setting], and we show the correspondence tracks $M$ rather
than $X$ itself." The final clause is what makes the paper theory-relevant
without overclaiming, and it should be paired with an explicit statement of what
the design cannot support. Reviewers punish descriptive papers that reach; they
reward the ones that name their own ceiling. Stating "we do not claim founder
origin is exogenous" in the paper is strictly better than having a reviewer
state it for you.

### Norms differ by field, and the difference is not subtle

This genre travels much better in *Organization Science*, *Strategic Management
Journal*, and *Strategy Science* than in *JM*, *JMR*, or *Marketing Science*,
where the descriptive lane is narrower and more codified. In marketing it runs
mainly through three channels: empirical generalizations, in which a regularity
is established across many datasets and contexts; new-data-source papers, in
which the contribution is a measurement capability and the first look it
affords; and stylized-facts sections embedded inside otherwise structural or
causal papers, where description motivates the model rather than standing alone.
@bronnenberg2009 is the canonical marketing-side exemplar of the standalone
form—a persistent geographic pattern in brand shares, a scaffold for
interpreting it, and no causal overclaim.

On the management side, *SMJ* publishes papers that name the genre in the
abstract. @liu2026ideology describe their study as taking a "question-driven
approach": does liberal institutional ownership show up in a firm's symbolic
climate actions, its substantive ones, or neither? The answer is reported as
associations, not effects, and several rows of @tbl-sw-descriptive are visible
in it. The antecedent comes from an external paper trail (the investors' political
donations), not from the authors' judgment. The cuts that carry the finding
(consistent donors, dedicated investors, firms without CEO duality) do the
off-diagonal work of showing where the pattern holds and where it fails. The
finding also turns on a dated split, 2016 onward, which the authors tie to rising
political polarization. Whether that break was fixed before the estimation is
exactly what the third row asks a reader to check, because a break chosen after
looking at the data is a forking path. The substance is developed in
@sec-mf-carbon.

The practical implication is a targeting decision made *before* writing. A
descriptive paper aimed at a marketing journal usually needs one of the three
channels above as its declared home; the same paper aimed at a management
journal can stand on the stylized-facts warrant directly. Authors who write the
management version and submit it to the marketing journal receive a predictable
review: interesting, but what is the identification?

A descriptive paper that stops at the pattern is one genre; a paper that goes on
to argue for a particular explanation of that pattern is another, and it needs a
reporting structure of its own. That is the subject of @sec-sw-peebi.

## The Abductive Paper and the PEEBI Structure {#sec-sw-peebi}

A descriptive paper stops at the pattern. A large class of empirical papers does
not: it commits to an *explanation* of the pattern that was constructed after the
pattern was seen, and that was never tested deductively because it did not exist
before the data did. This is abduction, or **inference to the best explanation**
(IBE), and it produces a great deal of what marketing knows. The difficulty is
not the inference—it is the *testimony*. @pillai2026peebi observe that although
scholars employ abduction routinely, there is no agreed-upon structure for
reporting it, and the hypo-deductive reporting template does not align with the
epistemology of abduction. They propose one, **PEEBI**, a five-section structure
in which the authors take prior knowledge and theories, establish the context and
observations worthy of interest, identify and evaluate candidate explanations for
the observed patterns, determine the best explanation and their reasoning for
accepting it, and abstract that explanation to a more generalizable theoretical
contribution. The structure "advances knowledge in a modest, stepwise fashion"
and is designed to foreground the author's judgment rather than hide it.

### Why the deductive template misreports abductive work

The template of @sec-sw-structure asks the reader to grant a chain that begins
with a hypothesis and ends with a test. Abductive work runs the other way: the
observation comes first, the candidate explanations are generated by the author
rather than handed down by prior theory, and the evidence that discriminates
among them is assembled afterward. @tbl-sw-abduction contrasts what each mode
actually asks of a reader.

| | Hypo-deductive paper | Abductive paper |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Where the claim comes from | Derived from theory *before* the data | Constructed to explain an observation *after* it |
| What the evidence does | Discriminates $H$ from $\neg H$ | Discriminates $E_k$ from the other candidates in a set the author assembled |
| What the reader grants | That the design could have falsified $H$ | That the candidate set is adequate and was evaluated evenhandedly |
| What failure looks like | The test does not reject | A rival explanation survives that the author did not consider |
| What must be disclosed | Design, measures, robustness | All of that, **plus** the order of discovery and the rejected candidates |
| Who does the judging | Nominally the data | Explicitly the author—and, if the paper is written well, the reader |

: What the two reporting modes ask of a reader. The last two rows are where the deductive template fails abductive work. {#tbl-sw-abduction}

Forcing abductive work into the deductive template requires a small fiction: the
explanation is presented as though it preceded the data. The field already has a
name for the vicious version of that fiction—HARKing—and the reason abduction is
*not* HARKing is disclosure: the order of discovery is stated, the rival
explanations are named, and the residual uncertainty is quantified or at least
bounded. The deductive template deletes precisely those three things. It does not
merely misfit the work; it removes the information that licenses the conclusion.

### The five acts

@tbl-sw-peebi states the five sections, what each one owes the reader, and where
it goes in a manuscript aimed at a marketing journal, since few marketing
editors will accept section headings named after an epistemology.

| Act | What the section does | What the reader is handed | Marketing manuscript home |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **P**riors | States the prior knowledge and theories the inquiry begins from | The baseline against which the observation is surprising | Introduction and a short theory-background section |
| **E**stablish | Establishes the context and the observations worthy of scholarly interest | The phenomenon itself: measurement, setting, and why the pattern is not an artifact | "Empirical setting" plus a stylized-facts or model-free-evidence section |
| **E**valuate | Identifies *and* evaluates candidate explanations for the observed pattern | The full candidate set and the evidence bearing on each | "Alternative explanations", promoted from appendix to spine |
| **B**est | Determines the best explanation and the reasoning for accepting it | The author's judgment, stated as judgment, with its grounds | "Discriminating evidence" or the analysis section that adjudicates |
| **I**mplication | Abstracts the best explanation into a more generalizable theoretical contribution | The claim that travels beyond this setting, and its boundary | General discussion and theoretical implications |

: The five PEEBI acts of @pillai2026peebi, with the marketing-manuscript section that hosts each. The letters index the five sections in the order the published account states them; the short act names here are our labels for the functions that account describes. {#tbl-sw-peebi}

The move that does the work is the third act. In a conventional marketing paper,
alternative explanations are a defensive appendix written to preempt reviewer
objections; in an abductive paper they are the argument. A reader who is shown
four candidates, the evidence for and against each, and the author's reasoning
for preferring one has been given the material to disagree—which is the point.
@pillai2026peebi frame this as elevating the reader's role: the paper's job is to
supply the information a reader needs to reach a judgment, not to foreclose it.

### The abductive chain

The counterpart to @eq-sw-chain runs

$$
\underbrace{O}_{\text{observation}} \;\Rightarrow\;
\underbrace{\mathcal{E} = \{E_1, \dots, E_K\}}_{\text{candidate set}} \;\Rightarrow\;
\underbrace{V}_{\text{evaluation}} \;\Rightarrow\;
\underbrace{E^{*}}_{\text{best explanation}} \;\Rightarrow\;
\underbrace{T}_{\text{abstraction}}
$$ {#eq-sw-abduction}

and, as before, every arrow is a claim the reader may refuse to grant. The
observation $O$ must be real and genuinely surprising against the priors—a
pattern that everyone expected is not an abductive trigger. The candidate set
$\mathcal{E}$ must be *adequate*: it must contain the explanation a hostile
expert would propose, which is the arrow that breaks most often. The evaluation
$V$ must apply the same standard to every candidate; searching hard for evidence
that supports $E_1$ and casually for evidence against it is the abductive
analogue of a rigged specification search. The selection $E^{*}$ must dominate
the survivors on stated grounds rather than on the author's enthusiasm. And the
abstraction $T$ must not outrun the case: one setting supports a mechanism claim,
not a law.

Failure at each arrow has a diagnostic signature in reviews. A weak $O$ draws
"this is well known." A thin $\mathcal{E}$ draws "the authors have not ruled
out..." An asymmetric $V$ draws "the evidence for the preferred story is treated
differently from the evidence against it." An overreaching $T$ draws "the
contribution is not supported by a single context."

### What makes an explanation "best"

The word *best* carries the whole burden, and @pillai2024lovely unpack it along
two dimensions that do not coincide. An explanation is **lovely** when it is
useful, general, and provides meaning; it is **likely** when it is close to the
truth. Loveliness is what makes a mechanism worth having; likeliness is what
makes it true. A managerially elegant story about why a promotion worked can be
extremely lovely and quite unlikely, and a precisely estimated coefficient can be
likely and entirely unlovely. Their argument is that interpreting observational
results requires an understanding of context that statistical analysis alone
cannot supply, and that historical methods—hermeneutics, contextualization, and
source criticism—help scholars both *generate* new candidate explanations and
*judge* and balance the virtues that make one explanation better than another.

In marketing the contextual sources are close at hand and systematically
underused: category and brand histories, trade press, retailer and manufacturer
archives, advertising archives, regulatory filings, and interviews with the
people who made the decisions in the data. A researcher who knows that a category
was restructured by a distribution change in 1998 has a candidate explanation
that no amount of panel-data variance decomposition will hand them.

The practical artifact this yields is a **candidate-explanation table**, written
early and revised as evidence accumulates. @tbl-sw-candidates sketches its form
for a stylized marketing pattern—a brand's share is persistently higher in
markets it entered first—and it is the single most useful document a student can
produce before writing an abductive paper, because it makes the completeness of
$\mathcal{E}$ visible to the author.

| Candidate explanation | Lovely? (useful, general, meaningful) | Likely? (evidence for) | Evidence against | Discriminating test available? |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Consumer-side brand capital formed early and persisting | High—travels to any repeat-purchase category | Share gap survives entry of national rivals | Cannot separate from supply-side with market-level data alone | Yes: observe consumers who move between markets |
| Supply-side cost or distribution advantage in early markets | Moderate—context-specific | Early entrant has denser distribution | Gap persists after distribution converges | Yes: control distribution and re-measure |
| Retailer assortment and shelf-space lock-in | Moderate | Assortment correlates with share | Pattern holds in categories with weak retailer power | Partly: cross-retailer variation |
| Advertising stock accumulated over decades | High | Cumulative spend correlates with share | Gap holds where historical spend was symmetric | Yes: historical ad-spend series |

: A candidate-explanation table for a stylized persistence pattern. The final column is the one that turns an essay into a paper. {#tbl-sw-candidates}

### A worked example, reconstructed

Marketing has abductive exemplars; what it lacks is the habit of labeling them.
Read as a two-paper arc, @bronnenberg2009 and @bronnenberg2012migration
instantiate the chain in @eq-sw-abduction almost exactly—though neither paper
presents itself in these terms, and the reconstruction is ours.

The first paper *establishes*: brand shares in consumer packaged goods differ
persistently across U.S. geographic markets, and the differences track the
brand's early entry more than a century back. Against the priors of a field that
models share as a function of current marketing mix, that is a genuine surprise,
and the paper states it as a pattern rather than as an effect. The candidate set
is the obvious one—something on the demand side (consumers in these markets
simply prefer this brand, for reasons formed long ago) versus something on the
supply side (the early entrant enjoys durable cost, distribution, or retail
advantages there).

Market-level data cannot separate those candidates, and this is where an
abductive paper either finds a discriminating observation or admits it cannot.
The second paper finds one: consumers who *move* between markets carry their
preferences with them, converging only slowly toward their new market's shares.
Movers separate the two candidates cleanly, because a consumer-side stock travels
with the consumer while a supply-side advantage does not. That is act four
performed in public—the best explanation determined, with the reasoning for
accepting it visible—and the abstraction in act five is the one that made the work
matter beyond CPG: brand preference behaves as an accumulated consumer-side
capital stock with a very long half-life.

Two features of the arc are worth copying. The discriminating evidence was
*sought after* the candidates were named, not before—the honest order, and the
one PEEBI asks you to report. And the abstraction stops where the evidence
stops: a claim about how preferences persist and transfer, not a claim that
early entry causes share everywhere.

### Getting an abductive paper through a marketing review

The genre travels less easily in *JM*, *JMR*, and *Marketing Science* than in
*SMJ* or *Organization Science*, for the reason given in @sec-sw-descriptive: the
default reviewer question in marketing is "what is the identification?" Three
adjustments carry most of the load.

Declare the design in the introduction. A sentence—"we do not test a
pre-specified hypothesis; we document a pattern, enumerate the explanations
consistent with it, and present evidence that discriminates among them"—costs
nothing and prevents the paper from being evaluated against a template it is not
using. Reviewers punish papers that appear to have failed at deduction far more
than papers that never attempted it.

Keep the conventional headings and put PEEBI underneath them, as in the last
column of @tbl-sw-peebi. The structure is a reporting discipline, not a demand
for new section names, and a manuscript that renames its sections after an
epistemology spends its first reviewer paragraph defending a formatting choice.

State the ceiling before a reviewer does. The abductive paper's ceiling is that
$\mathcal{E}$ may be incomplete, and the correct response is to say so and to
name what evidence would change the ranking. Papers that specify the observation
that would overturn their preferred explanation read as confident; papers that
imply the candidate set is exhaustive read as naive. This is the same principle
that governs the R&R response in @sec-review-process—make the reader's job of
disagreeing with you *easy*, and they will usually decline the invitation.

@fig-sw-peebi summarizes the flow, including the loop that the deductive template
has no way to represent: evaluation frequently sends the author back for more
candidates or more context, and the paper reports the end state of that loop
rather than pretending it did not run.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-sw-peebi
%%| fig-cap: "The PEEBI reporting structure for abductive work, after Pillai et al. (2026). The dashed arrows are the iteration the deductive template cannot represent: evaluation sends the author back for further candidates or further context, and the paper testifies to where that loop ended."
flowchart TD
    P["<b>P</b>riors<br/><i>prior knowledge and theories</i>"] --> E1["<b>E</b>stablish<br/><i>context and observations<br/>worthy of interest</i>"]
    E1 --> E2["<b>E</b>valuate<br/><i>identify and evaluate<br/>candidate explanations</i>"]
    E2 --> B["<b>B</b>est explanation<br/><i>and the reasoning<br/>for accepting it</i>"]
    B --> I["<b>I</b>mplication<br/><i>abstract to a generalizable<br/>theoretical contribution</i>"]
    E2 -.->|"candidate set inadequate"| E1
    B -.->|"no candidate dominates"| E2
    I -.->|"new priors for the next study"| P
    style E2 fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#1a73e8
    style B fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#1a73e8
```

### A checklist for the abductive manuscript

A reader finishing each act should be able to answer one question. If they
cannot, the act is not written yet.

- **After P**: what did we believe before, and why is the observation surprising
  against that belief?
- **After E (establish)**: is the pattern real—measured how, in what population,
  and robust to what obvious artifacts?
- **After E (evaluate)**: what else could produce this pattern, and what does
  the evidence say about each of those?
- **After B**: why this explanation rather than the runner-up, and what would
  change my mind?
- **After I**: what claim travels beyond this setting, and where does it stop?

The parallel exercise for a course is worth assigning directly: take a published
hypo-deductive paper in the student's area, reconstruct the abductive history
that almost certainly produced it, and rewrite the introduction in PEEBI form.
Students discover quickly that the reconstructed version is both more honest and
easier to read, which is the argument of @pillai2026peebi in miniature. The
seminar treatment of abduction as a mode of inference, alongside empirical
generalizations and stylized facts, is in @sec-theo-week05.

## The Decomposition Paper {#sec-sw-decomposition}

A third genre sits beside description and abduction, and it is the one most likely to
rescue a paper whose headline effect is small, imprecise, or already known. Its claim is
not "$X$ affects $Y$" but "$X$ affects $Y$ through these specific channels, which push in
opposite directions, in these proportions, under these conditions." The increment
$\Delta\mathcal{K}$ is the *anatomy* of an effect rather than its sign.

The genre is worth naming because the alternative is so common and so weak. A great many
papers—in marketing, economics, and management alike—end at a signed average: the
promotion raised sales, the technology cut employment, the entry helped the incumbent.
Signed averages age badly. They do not transfer to settings where the mixture of channels
differs, they cannot explain why two credible studies disagree, and they give a manager or
regulator nothing to act on beyond "more" or "less."

**The exemplar.** @clemens2026lowskill study a question with a long history of
irreconcilable estimates: does employing low-skill immigrants displace native workers? The
design is a natural firm-level randomization—the US H-2B visa quota is allocated in part
by federal lottery—paired with a pre-analysis plan and a purpose-built firm survey of 2021
lottery winners and losers. That alone would produce a signed average. What makes the paper
a template is that the signed average is *derived* rather than reported.

The authors write down a monopolistically competitive firm producing with immigrant labor
$I$, native low-skill labor $N$, capital $K$, and high-skill labor $H$ in a nested CES
technology [@ottaviano2012rethinking], facing demand elasticity $\eta$, with
immigrant–native substitution elasticity $\sigma$. Two mechanisms then run in opposite
directions. **Substitution**: immigrants and natives compete for the same tasks, so cheap
access to one displaces the other, and the force is governed by $\sigma$. **Scale**:
relaxing the hiring constraint lets the firm expand output, raising demand for every
input including native labor, and the force is governed by $\eta$. Stripping the model to
labor alone makes the arithmetic transparent: with $s_I$ and $s_N$ the immigrant and
native revenue shares, the effects of winning the lottery on revenue and on native
employment are
$$
\ln\frac{R_w}{R_\ell} \approx s_I \cdot
\frac{\eta - 1}{(\eta-1)(1-s_N) + (\sigma-1)s_N}\cdot \ln\frac{I_w}{I_\ell},
\qquad
\ln\frac{N_w}{N_\ell} \approx s_I \cdot
\frac{\eta - \sigma}{(\eta-1)(1-s_N) + (\sigma-1)s_N}\cdot \ln\frac{I_w}{I_\ell}.
$$ {#eq-sw-decomp}

The revenue effect is unambiguously non-negative. The employment effect has *indeterminate
sign*, positive when $\eta > \sigma$ and negative otherwise: whether immigrant hiring
crowds natives in or out is not a fact about immigrants but a race between two elasticities.
(With capital and high-skill labor restored, the crossing condition generalizes but keeps
the same structure.)

```{r sw-decomposition}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
# Effects of an exogenous increase in immigrant employment, from eq-sw-decomp.
s_I <- 0.20; s_N <- 0.65          # revenue shares of immigrant and native labor
grid <- expand.grid(eta = c(4, 8, 16), sigma = c(0.5, 1.5, 3, 6))

denom <- with(grid, (eta - 1) * (1 - s_N) + (sigma - 1) * s_N)
grid$revenue_effect  <- with(grid, s_I * (eta - 1)     / denom)
grid$native_effect   <- with(grid, s_I * (eta - sigma) / denom)
grid$verdict <- ifelse(grid$native_effect > 0, "crowds in", "crowds out")

round_df <- within(grid, {
  revenue_effect <- round(revenue_effect, 3)
  native_effect  <- round(native_effect, 3)
})
round_df[order(round_df$eta, round_df$sigma), ]
```

Every row has a positive revenue effect; the native-employment column flips sign inside the
same table. That single display carries more transferable knowledge than any average
treatment effect estimated from it, because a reader in a different industry can locate
their own $(\eta, \sigma)$ and read off the prediction. The paper's empirical estimates
then close the loop: losing the lottery cuts immigrant employment by 56% and contracts the
firm—revenue elasticity about $+0.16$, investment about $+1.03$ in the working-paper
version, with the published estimates in the range $0.20$--$0.22$ for production and
$1.5$--$2.1$ for investment—while the effect on US employment is zero or positive. Read
through @eq-sw-decomp, a null employment effect is not a non-result: it *identifies* the
substitution elasticity, which the authors back out at $0.8$--$2.2$, low relative to the
demand elasticity, which is exactly why scale wins.

**The four moves worth stealing.** The genre has a recognizable structure, and each move
is portable to a marketing paper.

1. **Write the model that makes the sign ambiguous.** The theory's job here is not to
   generate a directional hypothesis but to prove that direction *cannot* be signed a
   priori. That reframes a null or mixed result from a failure into an estimate of the
   parameter that decides the race.
2. **Turn the mechanism into a prespecified heterogeneity test.** The same model predicts
   *where* each channel should dominate—larger revenue effects for small firms facing more
   elastic demand, larger native-employment effects in rural areas where complementary
   workers have worse outside options—and both predictions were registered in advance and
   confirmed. Heterogeneity chosen after the fact is fishing; heterogeneity implied by the
   decomposition is a test.
3. **Recover the structural parameter from the reduced form.** The reduced-form
   coefficients are used to invert for $\sigma$, which is the quantity other studies argue
   about and the quantity that transfers.
4. **Say which quantity you estimated.** The authors distinguish the LATE recovered from
   the usual shift-share instruments—variation in immigrant *supply*, irrespective of
   current demand—from the policy-relevant treatment effect of a *policy-induced*
   restriction, and argue their lottery identifies the latter. Naming the estimand is
   itself a contribution when the literature has been silently averaging over several.

**Companion designs.** The decomposition move is not foreign to marketing; it is simply
underused as an explicit frame.

- Promotion analytics has run on decomposition for decades: a sales spike splits into
  brand switching, category expansion, purchase acceleration, and stockpiling, and the
  split—not the spike—determines incremental profit [@vanheerde2007; @guyt2014]
  (@sec-pricing).
- @biswas2026channel decompose the value of channel adoption by the *pathway* that
  produced it, isolating forward buying from habit persistence, and show the two mechanisms
  imply opposite corrections to incremental CLV (@sec-clv-pathways).
- @liu2026platform decompose the environmental effect of platform entry by market
  structure, finding that the entire average effect comes from dual-platform cities and
  none from single-platform ones (@sec-platform-entry-externality).
- @ellickson2023dml decompose a campaign's effect into the effects of its *components*
  with double machine learning, turning "the email worked" into which element of the email
  worked.
- In economics, the same instinct underwrites the task-based decomposition of automation
  into displacement and reinstatement effects, and the decomposition of trade shocks into
  substitution and scale channels; the shared feature is that the aggregate is written as
  a sum of forces with known signs before it is estimated.

**A field-experiment specimen.** The decomposition frame suits a firm-run randomized
experiment especially well, because a policy change seldom moves only one line of the
profit statement. @fang2026returnless worked with a leading global e-commerce platform
to test an agentic-AI refund policy on nearly one million customers. In the treatment
arm, an AI system evaluated the customer's multimodal evidence and offered a partial
refund with no return required. The control arm kept the standard process: ship the
item back for a full refund. No one could sign the net effect in advance, because the
components push in different directions. Refund payouts can rise. Processing costs
fall. Less hassle can raise long-run customer value. Strategic claiming is a cost. The
paper's economic framework writes the platform's payoff in terms of these drivers and
states the conditions under which the policy creates value. The experiment then signs
each one: payouts rise, processing costs fall, long-term customer value rises, and the
net effect on profit is positive. Treated customers go on to buy more, but they also
show signs of strategic behavior. The case adds two moves to the four above.

5. **Name the bundle.** The two arms differ in who decides (an AI agent or the
   standard process), in whether the item comes back, and in how much is refunded.
   The experiment identifies the effect of that policy as it would be deployed, not
   the effect of any one component, and the deployment effect is the quantity a
   platform deciding whether to deploy actually needs (@sec-causal-policy-lottery). A
   reader who wants the separate effect of returnlessness needs a different design,
   and saying so up front pre-empts the referee who would otherwise ask for it.
6. **Measure the downside.** Strategic behavior is the obvious objection to paying
   refunds without a return. Measuring it and pricing it into the net effect turns the
   referee's first question into one of the paper's findings.

The abstract is also a compact template for the genre. In order, it states the cost the
status quo imposes, on consumers in hassle and on firms in money; the technology that
makes a new policy feasible; the partner, the randomization, and the scale; the two
arms, each described as a complete policy; the framework; the sign of each payoff
component; the net effect; the countervailing risk; and the claim to novelty, here
"one of the first large-scale causal evaluations" of agentic AI in customer service.
The whole promise–payoff loop of @fig-sw-paper-flow, from problem to redeemed claim,
fits in fewer than two hundred words. (Only the abstract was accessible when this section was written; the
design details and effect sizes are in the paper.)

**Where it fails.** Two failure modes recur. The first is decomposition by regression
mediation with no design behind it: adding a mediator to a regression and reporting an
"indirect effect" decomposes nothing if the mediator is endogenous, and this remains the
most common way marketing papers claim mechanism without earning it. The second is
decomposing into channels the data cannot separate; if two mechanisms imply identical
predictions in every observable dimension, naming them both is rhetoric, not evidence. The
test to apply before writing is simple: for each channel in the decomposition, state the
observation that would change its estimated share. If no such observation exists, the
channel is not identified and the decomposition should be presented as an interpretation
rather than a result.

## The Effect–Mechanism–Boundary Paper {#sec-sw-emb}

A fourth architecture is now common enough in empirical strategy, marketing, and
information systems to be worth naming, because students imitate its surface without
understanding why it holds together. The paper establishes an effect, then explains
it, then bounds it—three stages that answer, in order, *whether*, *how*, and *for
whom*. @singh2026opensource is a well-built specimen and the running example here;
its substance is discussed in @sec-innovation.

**Stage 1 establishes the effect.** Firms adopting open-source product development
gained 4–5% in gross margin, estimated with staggered difference-in-differences and
replicated under a second DID estimator, generalized synthetic control, an
instrumental variable, and two dynamic panel estimators (@sec-causal-inference).

**Stage 2 explains it.** A moderated mediation model routes the effect through labor
productivity and shows the pathway is switched on by external contributor
participation (@sec-causal-mediation-firm-panel).

**Stage 3 bounds it.** A configurational analysis identifies the resource profiles
under which the gains actually appear, finding R&D intensity in every
high-profitability configuration (@sec-qual-fsqca).

### Why the stages are ordered, and why the method changes

The ordering is not stylistic. Each stage exists to answer the objection the previous
one provokes, which is the same architectural logic as the five-move template in
@sec-pwm-template. A reader shown a 4–5% margin gain immediately asks *through what*,
and a reader given a mediation pathway immediately asks *for which firms*. Reversing
the order strands the reader: a mechanism for an effect not yet established is a
story about nothing, and a boundary condition on an unexplained effect is a
subgroup table.

The subtler point, and the one students miss, is that **the method changes at every
stage because the question changes.** Quasi-experimental estimators answer a
counterfactual question about an average. Structural equation modeling answers a
question about a pathway's composition. Set-theoretic analysis answers a question
about which combinations of conditions travel with the outcome. Running one technique
through all three stages is a category error—a mediation model cannot establish an
average effect against selection, and a difference-in-differences cannot represent
equifinality. When a manuscript uses the same estimator throughout and merely adds
interaction terms, it usually has one stage wearing three hats.

Robustness follows the same principle: **put it where the identification is
weakest.** Their Stage 1 carries six estimators because that is where the causal
claim lives. Stage 2 gets a base-versus-full model comparison on AIC and BIC, a
5,000-replication bootstrap, and a second operationalization of the moderator. Stage 3
gets consistency thresholds and a separate analysis of the negated outcome. A uniform
robustness appendix applied indiscriminately to all three signals that the author has
not thought about which claim is actually fragile.

### The honesty requirement

The architecture has a built-in temptation, and resisting it is what separates the
good version from the imitation. **Identification strength declines across the
stages.** Stage 1 can be genuinely causal. Stage 2's mediator-to-outcome link
usually is not, because nothing randomized the mediator (@sec-causal-mediation-assumptions).
Stage 3 is set-theoretic description within a sample. A paper that presents all three
in the same confident register is overclaiming, and a careful referee will say so.
The fix costs one sentence per stage, stating what the design does and does not
support, and it buys the credibility the rest of the paper spends.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Is your Stage 2 load-bearing?

The diagnostic for whether the later stages are contributions or decoration: **would
a null there have changed the paper?** In the running example it would. Without the
mediation result, the 4–5% is a fact with no account of itself, equally consistent
with cost arbitrage—firms getting free labor—which the authors explicitly rule out
by showing that value accrues to firms with R&D rather than to firms with low
internal capacity. Without the configurational stage, the paper would recommend open
source to everyone, and its actual finding is that it pays only for firms able to
absorb what the community sends. If you cannot say what a null at Stage 2 or 3 would
have meant, those stages are robustness checks with ambitions, and a referee will
read them that way.
:::

When adapting this architecture, the marketing translation is usually
straightforward: an adoption or policy shock supplies Stage 1, a mediator the field
already measures well—satisfaction, salience, search effort, salesforce
productivity—supplies Stage 2, and the firm or customer heterogeneity the field
argues about supplies Stage 3. The binding constraint is almost always Stage 2,
because the mediator must be measured on the same units and at a frequency that lets
it sit causally between the shock and the outcome.

### A Second Specimen: When the Effect Is Already in Print {#sec-sw-emb-evcharging}

@chan2026evcharging, published online in JMR in 2026, uses the same three-stage
architecture under a harder starting condition, and the contrast with the running
example is instructive. Its question is whether a public EV charging station on a
supermarket's parking lot raises the store's revenue; the substance is in
@sec-geo-evcharging. The difficulty is that two earlier studies had already reported
that nearby chargers raise customer spending at US businesses, by about 5% and 3.2%
[@babar2024recharging; @zheng2024evstations], so the Stage 1 estimate of 3.4% could not
by itself be the contribution. This is the situation @sec-sw-decomposition describes, a
headline effect that is already known, and the paper is worth reading for how its front
end converts that effect into a contribution a marketing journal would publish.

**The funnel earns the question before it reaches the literature.** The introduction
opens on the retailer's opportunity rather than on energy policy: parking lots could
become charging hubs that relieve drivers' "charger anxiety", and the habitual,
high-frequency nature of grocery trips lines up with the recurring need to recharge. A
second paragraph shows practice moving, with European grocers and Walmart installing
chargers, and a third supplies the tension: penetration is still low, the grid and
permitting constraints behind the slow rollout are expected to ease, and no one knows
whether demand will materialize or through what mechanisms. The fourth paragraph makes
the move that turns this into a marketing paper. It sets aside the rent or revenue share
a retailer can earn from the charging operator and declares the grocer's focal interest
to be its core business; the data section later keeps charging income out of the
revenue measure, so the dependent variable matches the question. The same paragraph
discounts the existing evidence on grounds of credibility rather than absence: industry
reports that chargers lift sales lack causal identification, often come from parties
with a stake in the answer, and say nothing about mechanisms or boundary conditions.
Only then come the three research questions (effect, process, boundary conditions), one
paragraph of data and design, and three contributions that mirror the questions one for
one. Each contribution closes by naming who can act on it: retailers and policymakers
for the effect size, store managers for the process evidence, and managers rolling
chargers out across a chain for the heterogeneity. The abstract ends the same way.
@fig-sw-evcharging traces the chain.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-sw-evcharging
%%| fig-cap: "The argument chain of an effect-mechanism-boundary introduction, reconstructed from a 2026 JMR paper on EV charging at supermarkets. The retailer's opportunity and uncertainty motivate the question, a weak evidence base defines the gap, and each research question returns as a contribution addressed to a named decision maker."
flowchart LR
  subgraph SG1["Why it matters"]
    direction TB
    M1["Opportunity:<br/>parking lots as<br/>charging hubs"] --> M2["Practice moving,<br/>rollout still slow"]
    M2 --> M3["Retailer's question:<br/>effect on core sales?"]
  end
  subgraph SG2["Why it is still open"]
    direction TB
    G1["Industry claims:<br/>no causal design,<br/>vested interests"] --> G2["Two prior studies:<br/>card data, mixed<br/>US sectors"]
  end
  subgraph SG3["What the paper does"]
    direction TB
    D1["RQ1 effect<br/>RQ2 process<br/>RQ3 boundaries"] --> D2["300+ stores,<br/>staggered DiD"]
  end
  subgraph SG4["Who can act on it"]
    direction TB
    U1["Effect size:<br/>retailers, policymakers"] --> U2["Process:<br/>store managers"]
    U2 --> U3["Boundaries:<br/>chain roll-out managers"]
  end
  SG1 --> SG2
  SG2 --> SG3
  SG3 --> SG4
```

**Positioning against two predecessors is done in a table.** The literature section
grants the economics, transportation, and operations streams their own questions
(subsidies, optimal charger placement, the incentives of businesses to host chargers)
and narrows to the one that is open for a retailer: what hosting does to store
performance. The two predecessors are credited with showing that a positive effect is
possible, and a positioning table then lists study characteristics, process analyses,
and heterogeneity analyses as rows, with check marks showing where each earlier study
overlaps. That table is $\mathcal{K}_{\text{before}}$ made explicit, the remedy for the
annotated bibliography described in @sec-sw-front-end. Each empirical difference is tied
to a specific weakness rather than asserted as better data. Cross-sector averages may
hide sector heterogeneity, so the paper studies one sector to gain internal validity.
Third-party card data omit cash, and cashless payment is known to raise spending, so
retailer revenue including cash removes a possible bias. Foot-traffic counts include
people who buy nothing, so actual transactions replace them. Chargers anywhere nearby
give way to chargers on the retailer's own premises, which is what a retailer controls.
Germany complements the US evidence, and a staggered-robust estimator replaces two-way
fixed effects. The substantive gap is then grounded in what the earlier data
structurally could not show (a footnote notes they had no within-store variation across
categories), and the paper quotes each predecessor's own call for future research, one
for sales measured directly at the retailer and one for the underlying causes of the
spending effect, before stating that it answers both.

**The identification story is institutional first and tested second.** The case for
exogenous timing comes from how chargers actually get built. The retailer's management
explains that hardware shortages, grid capacity, and permits from several parties make
the go-live date unpredictable by anywhere from a few months to more than a year, and
operators racing to sign partnerships are not timing individual stores. The authors then
call their own approach conservative and test each way the claim could fail: model-free
before-and-after evidence first, then conditional parallel trends, pre-trend leads,
selection on observables, late adopters as controls, timing regressed on store traits, a
stacked synthetic-control design, alternative catchments and distance thresholds, and
named confounds (click and collect, pricing) checked one at a time.

**Stage 2 is built by decomposing the outcome, not by adding a mediator.** This is the
sharpest contrast with the running example and a direct answer to the binding constraint
just named. Rather than measure a mediator, the paper splits the outcome along its own
identity (revenue is transactions times average basket) and reruns the Stage 1 design on
each piece, then on transactions by weekday or weekend and peak or off-peak hour, on
promoted versus non-promoted sales, and on dozens of food categories. Two further tests
apply the same design to new contrasts: chargers equally close but off the store's lot,
and chargers added by a nearby rival, observed through the chain's untreated stores.
Because each of these tests inherits the Stage 1 identification, most of Stage 2 keeps
the causal register that the honesty requirement says mediation usually loses. The
exception is the last step, which regresses the category-level effects on category
traits such as impulse buying and ability to stockpile; that is association across
categories, and it should be read as such. What the decomposition delivers is concrete:
more transactions, unchanged basket size, and the largest gains in weekend off-peak
hours.

**Stage 3 reports the difference test, not just two subgroup estimates.** For every
median split the paper reports whether the two subgroup effects differ, and several do
not (absolute store size, distance to a main road, local charger density), which the
text states plainly; the euro translations in the appendix are restricted to splits
whose subgroups differ significantly. The register is less even between results and
summary. The market-stealing test yields ATT $= -0.0180$ ($p = 0.067$), and the authors
note that their data cannot quantify how much of the treated stores' gain came from
rivals; the abstract nonetheless reports "significant evidence for market stealing", and
the discussion says stealing contributes substantially. A reader who checks the summary
sentence against the table will notice the difference, and so will a referee. The
qualifier the table carries belongs in the sentence that summarizes it.

**The "so what" is priced in the reader's currency.** The 3.4% becomes roughly €200,000
a year for an average store. The discussion frames a "triple dividend": rent from the
operator, a higher top line, and demand spread more evenly across the week, which eases
staffing. A null result, that a category's environmental footprint does not predict its
uplift, is reported as a finding against an intuitive expectation. The research
implications place the paper in three marketing conversations: retail performance,
keeping physical stores relevant, and sustainability-oriented marketing. The published
version also carries an approved alternative disclosure plan, with proprietary data and
disguised data and code deposited with the journal's Data Editor, which is how a paper
built on one retailer's books meets JMR's replication policy.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Arguing for an effect someone else found first

1. Name the decision maker whose question this is, and choose the outcome that answers
   that question, even if it means excluding revenue the treatment also produces.
2. Treat earlier estimates as a baseline to sharpen. Tie each design difference to a
   specific bias or blind spot in the earlier measures, never to "better data" in
   general.
3. Ground the gap in what earlier data could not show, and quote the earlier authors'
   own calls for future research when they exist.
4. Put the positioning in a table a reviewer can audit at a glance.
5. Argue exogeneity from the process that sets the treatment date, then test each way
   that argument could fail.
6. If no mediator is measured on the right units at the right frequency, decompose the
   outcome and rerun the Stage 1 design on each component.
7. Report the difference test for every split, and keep the summary sentence in the
   same register as the table behind it.
8. End each contribution with the person who can act on it, and price it in that
   person's currency.
:::

### A Fourth Specimen: A Small Reward Framed as Four Open Questions {#sec-sw-emb-plasma}

@bruers2026plasma, published online in *Management Science* in 2026, is about as plain
as a field experiment gets. Four of twelve Red Cross-Flanders donation centers gave
plasma donors one extra thank-you coupon, worth about €1.50, for six months. There is
no structural model, no instrument, and no machine learning. The paper is worth reading
for how a modest manipulation became a contribution a general-interest journal would
take. It fits the three-stage architecture loosely. There is a randomized effect,
boundaries in time and across behaviors, and a mechanism stage built from a survey.
Published estimates below come from the article's abstract. Design details and
month-by-month estimates come from the KU Leuven dissertation chapter that first
reported the experiment [@bruers2024thesis]. Where the two versions differ, we say so.

**One experiment, four questions.** The dissertation chapter asked a collector's
question: how cost-effective are small material rewards for plasma donors? The
published version asks four questions about prosocial behavior in general. Each is
answered by a single feature of the design (@tbl-sw-plasma-questions). This is the move
most worth copying. A narrower paper would bury the information-only arm, the
month-by-month estimates, and the blood-donation outcome as robustness checks. Here
each becomes a headline result, because each answers a question the literature had
left open.

| Open question | Why a reader cannot guess the answer | Design feature that answers it | Published answer |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Do small rewards motivate prosocial behavior? | A payment small enough to seem token can lower effort below no payment at all [@gneezy2000payenough] | An extra coupon worth about €1.50, added to an existing coupon scheme | Plasma donations rise 7.1% over the reward period |
| How do short-run effects differ from longer-run adjustment? | Earlier randomized donor-incentive experiments ran for much shorter treatment periods | A 24-month donor panel: 11 months before treatment, 9 under it, 4 after | The reward effect grows over six months and disappears once the coupon is withdrawn |
| Do incentives pull effort away from other prosocial activities? | Displacement had been measured across nearby blood drives [@lacetera2012blood], not across the products one donor can give | Centers collect both blood and plasma, and only plasma earns the extra coupon | Blood donations fall 3.3% |
| Do reminders about existing rewards matter? | Donors may not know which coupons they already receive | A separate arm whose newsletter only states the existing coupons | Plasma donations rise 4.6% over nine months, an effect that fades with repetition |

: The anatomy of the framing in @bruers2026plasma. Questions and answers follow the published abstract. The second and third columns draw on the dissertation chapter's review and design [@bruers2024thesis]. {#tbl-sw-plasma-questions}

Each question also passes the test of @sec-sw-open-question: both answers would have
been publishable. A null on the first question would be evidence of crowding-out. A
drop below baseline after the coupon was withdrawn would have been a backlash result.
Zero substitution would mean the gain was net. The paper did not need any particular
sign to have a contribution, which is what made a small experiment safe to run for two
years.

**The long panel turns a small effect into a dynamics story.** @fig-sw-plasma-timeline
shows the schedule. The reward arm received the newsletter item for three months
before its extra coupon began, to accustom donors to seeing the coupons stated. Every
change was announced a month ahead. That staggering separates the reminder from the
reward within a single arm. The dissertation's monthly estimates trace the shape. The
reward effect climbs from 6.4% in January 2023 to 9.8% in June. The information effect
peaks at about 8% in the second and third months and falls to 0.8% by the ninth. The
versions disagree on one point. The dissertation reports a 4.4% effect in the first
month after withdrawal, which then fades. The published abstract says the effect
disappears immediately. Quote the version you cite.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-sw-plasma-timeline
%%| fig-cap: "The schedule of the plasma-reward experiment, from the dissertation chapter, with the effects the published abstract reports. Both treated arms received the newsletter item for nine months; only the reward arm received the third coupon, for the last six."
flowchart LR
  P["Pre-period<br/>Nov 2021 to Sep 2022<br/>11 months, no treatment"] --> I["Information only<br/>Oct to Dec 2022<br/>newsletter states the coupons<br/>in both treated arms"]
  I --> R["Reward period<br/>Jan to Jun 2023<br/>reward arm: 3 coupons<br/>for plasma instead of 2"]
  R --> Q["Post-period<br/>Jul to Oct 2023<br/>2 coupons again,<br/>no newsletter item"]
  I -.-> E1["Reminder: +4.6%<br/>over nine months,<br/>fading with repetition"]
  R -.-> E2["Extra coupon: +7.1% plasma,<br/>growing; blood -3.3%"]
  Q -.-> E3["Reward effect gone<br/>(published version)"]
```

The dissertation's appendix prints the monthly donation counts for each center, so the
picture can be redrawn from the page. @fig-sw-plasma-dynamics redraws it and fits the
dissertation's center-level robustness model: log monthly donations on center and month
fixed effects plus the two treatment indicators.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sw-plasma-dynamics
#| fig-cap: "Monthly plasma donations in the two treated arms relative to the control arm, rescaled so the eleven pre-experiment months average 1, redrawn from the center-level counts in the dissertation's appendix. Light shading marks the nine months in which the newsletter stated the coupons; dark shading marks the six months of the extra coupon in the reward arm."
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
# Monthly plasma donations at the 12 Red Cross-Flanders donation centers,
# November 2021 to October 2023, transcribed from Table 88 of the dissertation
# chapter that reports the experiment (Bruers 2024).
centers <- c("Aalst", "Brugge", "Edegem", "Geel",               # control
             "Genk", "Gent", "Mechelen", "Roeselare",           # information
             "Kortrijk", "Sint-Niklaas", "Turnhout", "Leuven")  # information + reward
arm <- rep(c("control", "information", "reward"), each = 4)
plasma <- matrix(c(
    625,  781, 1084,  493,  801, 1205,  570,  692,  945,  488,  535, 1274,  # Nov/21
    762, 1004, 1223,  681,  943, 1439,  746,  853, 1128,  647,  690, 1397,  # Dec/21

    747,  901, 1122,  628,  849, 1259,  667,  753,  971,  561,  605, 1333,  # Feb/22
    725,  942, 1201,  707,  822, 1339,  690,  859, 1033,  614,  658, 1368,  # Mar/22
    606,  754,  955,  572,  717, 1106,  572,  674,  947,  514,  534, 1137,  # Apr/22
    660,  888, 1125,  581,  819, 1327,  633,  718,  999,  517,  572, 1340,  # May/22

    768,  998, 1182,  698,  993, 1171,  825,  864, 1062,  639,  702, 1383,  # Jul/22

    771, 1018, 1199,  763, 1034, 1394,  878,  974, 1203,  699,  760, 1517,  # Sep/22
    648,  793,  982,  612,  757, 1225,  629,  764,  904,  498,  630, 1278,  # Oct/22
    710,  791,  989,  559,  876, 1277,  656,  772,  986,  567,  583, 1319,  # Nov/22
    719,  825,  923,  573,  807, 1311,  614,  784,  980,  590,  632, 1337,  # Dec/22
    657,  785,  975,  616,  815, 1124,  666,  800, 1005,  534,  640, 1356,  # Jan/23
    589,  834,  920,  571,  790, 1222,  599,  745, 1025,  577,  601, 1301,  # Feb/23
    741,  889,  959,  637,  810, 1286,  702,  872, 1093,  661,  697, 1454,  # Mar/23
    624,  749,  831,  500,  675, 1110,  523,  735,  983,  508,  564, 1214,  # Apr/23
    661,  802,  914,  537,  731, 1138,  601,  740,  997,  513,  632, 1244,  # May/23
    610,  819,  907,  543,  727, 1115,  531,  769, 1030,  551,  609, 1187,  # Jun/23

    896, 1148, 1401,  831,  873, 1573,  938, 1087, 1352,  736,  845, 1613,  # Aug/23
```
